source.title: Learning Deep Neural Networks under Agnostic Corrupted Supervision
source.authors: Boyang Liu; Mengying Sun; Ding Wang; P. Tan; Jia-Yu Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Tests training with corrupted labels and reports clean-test accuracy, but does not measure whether training error reaches zero.
record.gate_note: The experiments vary label corruption and report clean-test accuracy. They do not report training error, random-label test error at chance, training time to fit, or results for shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs. The random-label memorization statement in the Introduction is cited prior work, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study develops methods to mitigate corrupted supervision and evaluates clean-test performance. It invokes random-label memorization and zero training loss from Zhang et al., but reports no training-set fit or memorization measurements. Clean-test degradation alone does not establish V4's joint claim that networks fit the corrupted training set perfectly while generalization degrades.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that their gradient-filtering algorithms provide theoretical robustness guarantees and effective empirical performance under agnostic supervision corruption. They do not independently demonstrate fitting completely random labels.
record.recipe_differences: The study filters or reweights training examples using gradient-based criteria under several label-corruption schemes; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies with dataset, corruption type, corruption rate, and training method. The authors also report sensitivity to overestimating or underestimating the corruption rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports declining clean-test accuracy for standard training as symmetric corruption increases from 30% to 70%: 63.22% to 24.12% on CIFAR10 and 32.83% to 9.93% on CIFAR100. These results measure generalization under noise, without establishing fitting of corrupted labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard CNN clean-test accuracy decreases as symmetric training-label corruption increases over the tested intermediate rates.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed gradient-filtering methods improve clean-test performance under several supervision corruptions; Table 4 evaluates sensitivity to the assumed corruption rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filtering examples by loss-layer gradient norms can improve robustness to corrupted supervision.

record.problems: No training-error results are reported for the corruption experiments. The flattened tables make some values difficult to assign confidently to individual methods or conditions.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports clean-test accuracies across methods and corruption conditions, but the supplied table is flattened and does not reliably preserve method-to-value alignment; no rows were extracted. Table 4 has the same assignment limitation.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus real labels and convergence speed as corruption increases. Table 5 compares methods' epoch runtimes under one corruption condition, not time to fit across corruption rates.
Training-set fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training-set fit throughout increasing corruption and the complete progression from no corruption to fully random labels. Clean-test accuracy is reported at intermediate corruption rates, without measurements establishing simultaneous memorization.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are fitted before noisy labels. The reported training curves track test performance rather than separate learning of clean and corrupted training labels.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's tests/T2 designation and V4 tested status. Section 3.6 assumes zero training loss using cited prior work. The supplied tables preserve method headings and ordered condition lists sufficiently to recover Table 2's standard-training values; blanket claims that those values cannot be assigned are overstated. Tables 2 and 4 are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, with test error at chance and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random versus true labels, and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels grows.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The study reports test accuracy under several label-corruption rates but does not report training error or whether training remains perfect. The table values are flattened, so separate numerical rows are not reliably assignable to particular conditions.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect fitting random labels or generalization on true labels.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels during training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Random-label memorization motivates the method; zero training loss is assumed from Zhang et al., rather than independently tested. Reported empirical outcomes concern clean-test performance and method runtime.

tranche.reason: Section 3.6 uses cited zero-training-loss capacity in its comparison of loss and gradient filtering. The study evaluates corruption mitigation without measuring random-label fitting.

source_check.notes: No missing results bearing on V1–V6 were found. Testing curves do not measure training-set memorization; runtime comparisons concern filtering methods, not random versus true labels.
